claim: ADGRG1 (also known as GPR56) is an evolutionarily conserved regulator of OL development in humans, mice, and zebrafish.
source: The adhesion G protein-coupled receptor ADGRG1 (also known as GPR56) is an evolutionarily conserved regulator of OL development in humans, mice, and zebrafish, although its activating ligand for OL lineage cells is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing ADGRG1's role across species.

claim: The activating ligand for ADGRG1 in OL lineage cells is unknown.
source: The adhesion G protein-coupled receptor ADGRG1 (also known as GPR56) is an evolutionarily conserved regulator of OL development in humans, mice, and zebrafish, although its activating ligand for OL lineage cells is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Microglia-derived transglutaminase-2 (TG2) signals to ADGRG1 on OL precursor cells (OPCs) in the presence of the ECM protein laminin.
source: Here, we report that microglia-derived transglutaminase-2 (TG2) signals to ADGRG1 on OL precursor cells (OPCs) in the presence of the ECM protein laminin and that TG2/laminin-dependent activation of ADGRG1 promotes OPC proliferation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TG2/laminin-dependent activation of ADGRG1 promotes OPC proliferation.
source: Here, we report that microglia-derived transglutaminase-2 (TG2) signals to ADGRG1 on OL precursor cells (OPCs) in the presence of the ECM protein laminin and that TG2/laminin-dependent activation of ADGRG1 promotes OPC proliferation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including in vitro proliferation assays.

claim: Signaling by TG2/laminin to ADGRG1 on OPCs improves remyelination in two murine models of demyelination.
source: Signaling by TG2/laminin to ADGRG1 on OPCs additionally improves remyelination in two murine models of demyelination.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cuprizone and LPC demyelination models.

claim: OPCs are abundant in the adult CNS, generating new oligodendrocytes and new myelin under conditions of myelin damage.
source: OPCs are abundant in the adult CNS, generating new oligodendrocytes and new myelin under conditions of myelin damage, as is seen in demyelinating diseases and in rodent models of demyelination.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about OPC biology.

claim: The regenerative capacity of OPCs after injury is poor.
source: Unfortunately, the regenerative capacity of OPCs after injury is poor, necessitating further investigation into the molecular mechanisms that guide both developmental and post-injury induced OPC differentiation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of myelin repair.

claim: Cell-cell interactions with microglia influence OPC proliferation and maturation.
source: Cell-cell interactions with other glial populations, in particular microglia, influence OPC proliferation and maturation (Hagemeyer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Nonspecific suppression of microglial function with minocycline leads to a reduction in the numbers of neural progenitors and OPCs during postnatal CNS development.
source: For example, the nonspecific suppression of microglial function with the anti-inflammatory drug minocycline leads to a reduction in the numbers of neural progenitors and OPCs during postnatal CNS development, suggesting that a cell-cell interaction is critical to the maturation of the OL-lineage (Shigemoto-Mogami et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Clearance of damaged myelin by microglia is necessary for OPC-dependent remyelination in toxin-induced murine models of demyelination.
source: By comparison, crosstalk between OPCs and microglia has been widely reported in the context of demyelinating insults (Miron et al., 2013), including in demyelinating diseases such as toxin-induced murine models of demyelination in which clearance of damaged myelin by microglia is necessary for OPC-dependent remyelination (Kotter et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Most aGPCRs possess a GPCR-Autoproteolysis-INducing (GAIN) domain that mediates autoproteolytic processing during protein maturation to generate an N- and a C-terminal fragment (NTF and CTF, respectively), which remain non-covalently associated on the cell surface.
source: Most aGPCRs possess a GPCR-Autoproteolysis-INducing (GAIN) domain that mediates autoproteolytic processing during protein maturation to generate an N- and a C-terminal fragment (NTF and CTF, respectively), which remain non-covalently associated on the cell surface (Langenhan et al., 2013; Hamann et al., 2015; Langenhan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about aGPCR structure supported by citations.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in ADGRG1 cause bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria (BFPP), which includes CNS hypomyelination.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in ADGRG1 cause the devastating human brain malformation called bilateral frontoparietal polymicrogyria (BFPP), which is comprised of a constellation of structural brain defects including CNS hypomyelination (Piao et al., 2004; Piao et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on human genetics.

claim: Conditional deletion of Adgrg1 in OL lineage cells results in CNS hypomyelination.
source: Conditional deletion of Adgrg1 in OL lineage cells results in CNS hypomyelination, and this is specifically caused by deficiencies in ADGRG1 signaling in OPCs and immature OLs (Giera et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Loss of Adgrg1 in mice and zebrafish decreases OPC proliferation, leading to a reduced number of mature myelinating OLs and fewer myelinated axons in the CNS.
source: Loss of Adgrg1 in mice and zebrafish decreases OPC proliferation, thereby leading to a reduced number of mature myelinating OLs and fewer myelinated axons in the CNS (Ackerman et al., 2015; Giera et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Approximately 80% of Iba1+ microglia express putative ligand of ADGRG1 at P5.
source: Quantitative analyses showed that ~80% Iba1 +microglia and~20% of GFAP +astrocytes express the putative ligand of ADGRG1 (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Approximately 20% of GFAP+ astrocytes express putative ligand of ADGRG1 at P5.
source: Quantitative analyses showed that ~80% Iba1 +microglia and~20% of GFAP +astrocytes express the putative ligand of ADGRG1 (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: No obvious putative ligand binding was detected in OPCs at P5.
source: We observed robust and consistent putative ligand detection in microglia (Figure 1B and C), while no obvious putative ligand binding was detected in OPCs and only sparse signals were observed in astrocytes (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: TG2 is a known binding partner of ADGRG1 in melanoma cells.
source: We first focused our attention on TG2 because it is a known binding partner of ADGRG1 in melanoma cells (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Tgm2 knockout mice have significantly reduced numbers of Plp+ OLs in the corpus callosum at P14 compared to littermate controls.
source: Indeed, we observed significantly reduced numbers of Plp+ OLs in the CC of Tgm2 knockout mice at both P14 and P28 compared to littermate controls (Figure 2A and B), with reductions in Plp+ OLs that are similar to reductions observed in Adgrg1 knockout mice (Giera et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Tgm2 knockout mice have significantly reduced numbers of Plp+ OLs in the corpus callosum at P28 compared to littermate controls.
source: Indeed, we observed significantly reduced numbers of Plp+ OLs in the CC of Tgm2 knockout mice at both P14 and P28 compared to littermate controls (Figure 2A and B), with reductions in Plp+ OLs that are similar to reductions observed in Adgrg1 knockout mice (Giera et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Four- to five-month-old Tgm2 knockout mice showed normal levels of Plp+ OLs.
source: Similar to our analysis of callosal Plp+ OL density in adult Adgrg1-deficient mice (Giera et al., 2015) and consistent with a previous analysis of two-month-old Tgm2-deficient mice (Van Strien et al., 2011), four- to five-month-old Tgm2 knockout mice showed normal levels of Plp+ OLs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), indicating a gradual correction of OL numbers through adulthood.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citations to prior work.

claim: P28 Tgm2-/- mice have significantly fewer myelinated axons in the corpus callosum compared to littermate controls.
source: Transmission electron microscopy of P28 CC showed significantly fewer myelinated axons in Tgm2-/- mice compared to littermate controls (Figure 2C and D), whereas myelin thickness corrected for axon caliber (g-ratio), total axon numbers, and axon diameters were comparable between the two groups of animals (Figure 2E, Figure 2-figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Myelin thickness corrected for axon caliber (g-ratio) is comparable between P28 Tgm2-/- mice and controls.
source: Transmission electron microscopy of P28 CC showed significantly fewer myelinated axons in Tgm2-/- mice compared to littermate controls (Figure 2C and D), whereas myelin thickness corrected for axon caliber (g-ratio), total axon numbers, and axon diameters were comparable between the two groups of animals (Figure 2E, Figure 2-figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2-figure supplement 2.

claim: Total axon numbers are comparable between P28 Tgm2-/- mice and controls.
source: Transmission electron microscopy of P28 CC showed significantly fewer myelinated axons in Tgm2-/- mice compared to littermate controls (Figure 2C and D), whereas myelin thickness corrected for axon caliber (g-ratio), total axon numbers, and axon diameters were comparable between the two groups of animals (Figure 2E, Figure 2-figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 2.

claim: Axon diameters are comparable between P28 Tgm2-/- mice and controls.
source: Transmission electron microscopy of P28 CC showed significantly fewer myelinated axons in Tgm2-/- mice compared to littermate controls (Figure 2C and D), whereas myelin thickness corrected for axon caliber (g-ratio), total axon numbers, and axon diameters were comparable between the two groups of animals (Figure 2E, Figure 2-figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2-figure supplement 2.

claim: Tgm2 is primarily expressed by microglia in postnatal murine CNS cells.
source: Recent transcriptomic studies revealed that Tgm2 is primarily expressed by microglia in postnatal murine CNS cells (Zhang et al., 2014), with expression detected in purified embryonic, early postnatal, and adult microglia (Matcovitch-Natan et al., 2016) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior transcriptomic studies and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Western blot analysis of freshly isolated, purified murine glial cells demonstrated selective enrichment of TG2 in microglia, with no detectable TG2 protein in wildtype OPCs, OLs, astrocytes, or Tgm2-/- microglia.
source: Consistent with these reports, our western blot analysis of freshly isolated, purified murine glial cells demonstrated selective enrichment in microglia, with no detectable TG2 protein in wildtype OPCs, OLs, astrocytes, or Tgm2-/- microglia (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The numbers of Plp+ OLs in the corpus callosum of microglia-specific Tgm2 knockout mice (Tgm2fl/fl;Cx3cr1Cre+) were significantly reduced compared to littermate controls at P28.
source: The numbers of Plp+ OLs in the CC of microglia-specific Tgm2 knockout mice (Tgm2fl/fl;Cx3cr1Cre+) were significantly reduced compared to littermate Tgm2fl/+;Cx3cr1Cre- controls (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: The reduction in Plp+ OLs in microglia-specific Tgm2 knockout mice is comparable to what was observed in the constitutive Tgm2 knockout at P28.
source: Importantly, the reduction is comparable to what was observed in the constitutive Tgm2 knockout at P28 (Figure 2A and B), supporting the hypothesis that microglia are the primary source of TG2 during OL development.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data from Figure 2G-H with Figure 2A-B.

claim: Numbers of Pdgfra+ OPCs in the corpus callosum of Tgm2-/- mice were significantly reduced compared to controls at P14.
source: Indeed, numbers of Pdgfra+ OPCs in the CC of Tgm2-/- mice were significantly reduced compared to controls at P14 (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Loss of Adgrg1 in the OL lineage causes premature cell cycle exit, resulting in a diminished size of Pdgfra+ OPC pools and fewer mature OLs.
source: Our previous studies showed that loss of Adgrg1 in the OL lineage causes premature cell cycle exit, resulting in a diminished size of Pdgfra+ OPC pools and fewer mature OLs (Giera et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: There are significantly fewer BrdU+/Ki67+ double positive cells in the corpus callosum of Tgm2 knockouts compared to controls at P14.
source: Therefore, we performed cell cycle exit assays (Figure 3C) and found significantly fewer BrdU+/Ki67+ double positive cells in the CC of Tgm2 knockouts compared to the controls (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: There is an overall reduction in BrdU+ cells in the corpus callosum of Tgm2 knockout mice compared to littermate controls at P14.
source: Consistent with decreased OPC proliferation, we also observed an overall reduction in BrdU+ cells (Figure 3F) and fewer PDGFRα+/BrdU+ OPCs in Tgm2 knockout mice compared to littermate controls (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There are fewer PDGFRα+/BrdU+ OPCs in Tgm2 knockout mice compared to littermate controls at P14.
source: Consistent with decreased OPC proliferation, we also observed an overall reduction in BrdU+ cells (Figure 3F) and fewer PDGFRα+/BrdU+ OPCs in Tgm2 knockout mice compared to littermate controls (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: OPCs prematurely exit the cell cycle in the absence of TG2.
source: We conclude that OPCs prematurely exit the cell cycle in the absence of TG2, as we previously reported in Adgrg1-/- mice (Giera et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the cell cycle exit assay data and comparison to prior work on Adgrg1.

claim: Recombinant TG2 (rTG2) failed to enhance the proliferation of wildtype OPCs grown on poly-D-lysine.
source: To our surprise, rTG2 failed to enhance the proliferation of wt OPCs grown on poly-D-lysine (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: TG2 is present in the extracellular milieu and is capable of cross-linking ECM proteins, including laminin-111.
source: TG2 is present in the extracellular milieu and is capable of cross-linking ECM proteins, including laminin-111 (Aeschlimann et al., 1992; Belkin, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Laminins are broadly detected in the postnatal corpus callosum and in close proximity with OPCs in vivo.
source: In light of this interaction, and the observation that laminins are broadly detected in the postnatal CC and in close proximity with OPCs in vivo (Relucio et al., 2012), we tested the need for laminin-111 in promoting OPC proliferation in a ADGRG1- and TG2-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: OPC proliferation was significantly increased in the presence of both rTG2 and laminin-111, but not in cells exposed to either protein alone.
source: We found that OPC proliferation was significantly increased in the presence of both rTG2 and laminin-111, but not in cells exposed to either protein alone (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Fibronectin did not enhance OPC proliferation in the presence of rTG2.
source: Fibronectin, another ECM protein expressed in the CNS and crosslinked by TG2 (Lorand et al., 1988), did not enhance OPC proliferation in this assay (Figure 3I), suggesting specificity for laminin-111.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: TG2-induced OPC proliferation in the presence of laminin-111 required the enzymatic crosslinking activity of TG2.
source: Indeed, TG2-induced OPC proliferation in the presence of laminin-111 required the enzymatic crosslinking activity of TG2, as transamidation-inactive TG2-W241A mutant protein (Pinkas et al., 2007) failed to promote OPC proliferation (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation assay data using enzymatically dead TG2 mutant shown in Figure 3J.

claim: rTG2 did not promote proliferation of Adgrg1-/- OPCs in the presence of laminin-111.
source: To confirm that TG2 regulates OPC proliferation in a ADGRG1-dependent manner, we cultured OPCs derived from P5 Adgrg1+/+ or Adgrg1-/- mice in the presence of laminin-111, with or without rTG2. rTG2 did not promote proliferation of Adgrg1-/- OPCs (Figure 3K), further supporting a ADGRG1-dependent TG2 function on OPC proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro proliferation assay data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) regulates OPC cell cycle progression.
source: Cyclin-dependent kinase 2 (CDK2) regulates OPC cell cycle progression (Belachew et al., 2002; Jablonska et al., 2007), and we previously reported reductions in CDK2 protein levels in Adgrg1-null OPCs (Giera et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Western blot analysis of CDK2 in acutely isolated OPCs from P6 Tgm2-/- mice showed significantly decreased levels of CDK2 protein compared to littermate controls.
source: Indeed, western blot analysis of CDK2 in acutely isolated OPCs from P6 Tgm2-/- mice showed significantly decreased levels of CDK2 protein compared to littermate controls (Figure 3L and M).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3L and M.

claim: RhoA is a regulator of cell cycle progression.
source: An additional regulator of cell cycle progression is RhoA (Chircop, 2014), which was recently reported to function downstream of ADGRG1 activation in OPCs (Ackerman et al., 2015; Giera et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Active RhoA was significantly reduced in Tgm2-/- corpus callosum compared to controls.
source: Using a pull-down assay to specifically isolate activated RhoA in corpus callosal tissue of Tgm2-/- mice and littermate controls, we found that active RhoA was significantly reduced in Tgm2-/- CC (Figure 3N and O).
evidence: This is supported by RhoA pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3N and O.

claim: Tgm2 is highly expressed in purified adult microglia.
source: The finding that Tgm2 is highly expressed in purified adult microglia, and that this expression is not diminished in a murine model of MS additionally motivated us (Wlodarczyk et al., 2017) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Tgm2 knockout mice exhibit impaired remyelination following cuprizone exposure.
source: Moreover, a previous report showed that Tgm2 knockout mice exhibit impaired remyelination following cuprizone exposure (Van Strien et al., 2011), leading us to hypothesize that the relevant OPC receptor for TG2 might be ADGRG1 in this remyelination model.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Quantitative morphometry of Black-Gold-stained myelin revealed a significant decrease in remyelination at 7 and 10 days recovery in the corpus callosum of mice lacking Adgrg1 in OPCs compared with control littermates after cuprizone treatment.
source: Quantitative morphometry of Black-Gold-stained myelin revealed a significant decrease in remyelination at 7 and 10 DR in the CC of mice lacking Adgrg1 in OPCs compared with control littermates (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Black-Gold myelin staining data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The reduction in myelin after cuprizone treatment was accompanied by a reduction in the number of myelinating OLs in mice lacking Adgrg1 in OPCs.
source: As we observed during CNS development, this reduction in myelin was accompanied by a reduction in the number of myelinating OLs (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mice lacking Adgrg1 in OPCs had reduced numbers of myelinating OLs in the lesion 14 days post-LPC injection.
source: In the focal de-/re-myelination model using injections of lysophosphatidylcholine (LPC) into the external capsule of the CC (Hammond et al., 2015) to create lesions, mice lacking Adgrg1 in OPCs had reduced numbers of myelinating OLs in the lesion 14 dpl (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Microglia-specific Tgm2 knockout mice had fewer myelinated axons in the lesion compared to control mice 14 days post-LPC injection.
source: Additionally, in the same LPC injection model, microglia-specific Tgm2 knockout mice had fewer myelinated axons in the lesion compared to control mice (Figure 4F and G), while g-ratio was unaffected (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: G-ratio was unaffected in microglia-specific Tgm2 knockout mice 14 days post-LPC injection.
source: Additionally, in the same LPC injection model, microglia-specific Tgm2 knockout mice had fewer myelinated axons in the lesion compared to control mice (Figure 4F and G), while g-ratio was unaffected (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Remyelination was significantly impaired in cerebellar slices derived from OPC-specific Adgrg1-null mice after LPC-induced demyelination.
source: Demyelination was induced by a 24 hr exposure to LPC, and after four days recovery we observed robust remyelination in wt cerebellar slices. By comparison, this remyelination was significantly impaired in cerebellar slices derived from OPC-specific Adgrg1-null mice (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by organotypic slice culture data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: rTG2 increased myelination in both wildtype and Tgm2 single knockout cerebellar slices with 4 days of daily treatments.
source: Indeed, rTG2 increased myelination in both wt and Tgm2 single knockout cerebellar slices with 4 days of daily treatments (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by organotypic slice culture data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Increased remyelination by rTG2 was not observed in Tgm2/Adgrg1 double knockout slices.
source: Excitingly, this effect appeared to be ADGRG1-dependent as increased remyelination was not observed in Tgm2/Adgrg1 double knockout slices (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by organotypic slice culture data shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: The interaction between ADGRG1 and TG2 regulates efficient remyelination following cuprizone- and LPC-mediated injury.
source: Taken together, the interaction between ADGRG1 and TG2 regulates efficient remyelination following cuprizone- and LPC-mediated injury.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of the remyelination experiments.

claim: Laminin regulates oligodendrogenesis and CNS myelination by interacting with integrins and dystroglycan.
source: It is known that laminin regulates oligodendrogenesis and CNS myelination by interacting with integrins and dystroglycan (Colognato and Tzvetanova, 2011; Colognato et al., 2004; Colognato et al., 2007; Colognato et al., 2002) and promotion of OPC proliferation in vivo (Relucio et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: TG2 is a member of the transglutaminase protein family that functions as crosslinking enzymes to ligate proteins between the ε-amino group of a lysine residue and the γ-carboxamide group of a glutamine residue.
source: TG2 is a member of the transglutaminase protein family; family members including TG2 function as crosslinking enzymes to ligate proteins between the ε-amino group of a lysine residue and the γ-carboxamide group of a glutamine residue (Fesus and Piacentini, 2002; Lai et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about TG2 biochemistry supported by citations.

claim: TG2 can be found both in the intracellular and the extracellular spaces of various types of tissues.
source: Unlike other members of the transglutaminase family, TG2 can be found both in the intracellular and the extracellular spaces of various types of tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TG2 localization.

claim: The intracellular portion of TG2 is thought to predominantly act as a signaling molecule that requires its GTPase activity.
source: The intracellular portion of TG2 is thought to predominantly act as a signaling molecule that requires its GTPase activity (Nakaoka et al., 1994), whereas the extracellular portion of TG2 binds to proteins of the ECM and exerts its crosslinking enzymatic activity (Belkin, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The extracellular portion of TG2 binds to proteins of the ECM and exerts its crosslinking enzymatic activity.
source: The intracellular portion of TG2 is thought to predominantly act as a signaling molecule that requires its GTPase activity (Nakaoka et al., 1994), whereas the extracellular portion of TG2 binds to proteins of the ECM and exerts its crosslinking enzymatic activity (Belkin, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A single missense mutation (W241A) in the catalytic core of TG2 specifically abolishes its crosslinking enzymatic activity with other functions preserved.
source: A single missense mutation (W241A) in the catalytic core of TG2 specifically abolishes its crosslinking enzymatic activity with other functions preserved (Pinkas et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TG2 binds laminin-111.
source: It was previously reported that TG2 binds laminin-111 (Aeschlimann et al., 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Recent reports have described differences in gene expression, morphology, and metabolism of grey and white matter microglia and OPCs.
source: Recent reports have described differences in gene expression, morphology, and metabolism of grey and white matter microglia and OPCs (Hagemeyer et al., 2017; Young et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of ADGRG1 does not cause as drastic OL development phenotypes compared to loss of other receptors such as GPR17.
source: It is worth noting that loss of ADGRG1 does not cause as drastic OL development phenotypes compared to loss of other receptors such as GPR17 (Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior work supported by citation.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in ADGRG1 manifest as CNS hypomyelination in humans.
source: Although perturbations to the ADGRG1-TG2 pathway had mild effects on in vitro OPC proliferation, loss-of-function mutations in ADGRG1 manifest as CNS hypomyelination in humans (Giera et al., 2015; Piao et al., 2005; Piao et al., 2004), underscoring the importance of understanding ADGRG1 function in OL lineage cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pharmacological and biological modulators of ADGRG1 activity have recently been identified.
source: Pharmacological and biological modulators of ADGRG1 activity have recently been identified (Stoveken et al., 2016; Salzman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: aGPCR ligand binding is solely mediated by its N-terminal fragment (NTF).
source: aGPCR ligand binding is solely mediated by its N-terminal fragment (NTF)(Hamann et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about aGPCR structure-function supported by citation.

claim: Putative ADGRG1 binding proteins were labeled in P5 mouse corpus callosum tissue using ADGRG1N-hFc probe.
source: To establish the distribution of an OPC-specific ADGRG1 ligand in the developing brain, we labeled putative ADGRG1 binding proteins in mouse corpus callosum (CC) tissue with a probe comprised of the ADGRG1 NTF fused to human immunoglobulin Fc fragment (ADGRG1N-hFc; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: Robust and consistent putative ligand detection was observed in microglia at P5.
source: We observed robust and consistent putative ligand detection in microglia (Figure 1B and C), while no obvious putative ligand binding was detected in OPCs and only sparse signals were observed in astrocytes (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Only sparse putative ligand signals were observed in astrocytes at P5.
source: We observed robust and consistent putative ligand detection in microglia (Figure 1B and C), while no obvious putative ligand binding was detected in OPCs and only sparse signals were observed in astrocytes (Figure 1D–G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1D-G.

claim: Biotinylated ADGRG1N-hFc was used to purify ADGRG1 binding partner(s) from mixed glial cell lysate enriched in microglia and astrocytes.
source: Biotinylated ADGRG1N-hFc was incubated with protein lysates isolated from cultured primary glial cells that were enriched for microglia and astrocytes, and streptavidin beads were used to capture biotinylated ADGRG1 and its glial-derived candidate binding partner(s) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used for proteomics.

claim: Mass spectrometry identified Plectin, Transglutaminase 2, ADGRG1, Growth arrest-specific 6, and other proteins as putative ADGRG1 binding partners.
source: Purified complexes were then submitted for identification by mass spectrometry following digestion by trypsin. Proteins with more than five identified tryptic peptides from three independent experiments are listed in Table 1.
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Table 1.

claim: TG2 is a known binding partner of ADGRG1 in melanoma cells.
source: We first focused our attention on TG2 because it is a known binding partner of ADGRG1 in melanoma cells (Xu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: No gene dosage effect was apparent for Tgm2, as no difference in the density of Plp+ OLs or the percentage of myelinated axons in corpus callosum was detected between Tgm2+/+ and Tgm2+/- mice.
source: A gene dosage effect was not apparent, as we detected no difference in the density of Plp+ OLs or the percentage of myelinated axons in CC between Tgm2+/+ and Tgm2+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Whole mount in situ hybridization for myelin basic protein (mbp) at 5 days post-fertilization did not reveal CNS myelination phenotypes in zebrafish mutants of gas6, mpp6a, mpp6b, pleca, or plecb.
source: Whole mount in situ hybridization (WISH) for myelin basic protein (mbp) at 5 days post-fertilization did not reveal CNS myelination phenotypes in any of the putative-ligand zebrafish mutants at this stage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F–O), a time point at which adgrg1 zebrafish mutants exhibit reduced mbp expression (Ackerman et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by whole mount in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F-O.

claim: The lack of myelination phenotype in zebrafish mutants of gas6, mpp6a, mpp6b, pleca, and plecb suggested that these proteins do not function as ligands for ADGRG1 during OPC development.
source: This lack of phenocopy suggested that Gas6, Mpp6, and Plectin do not function as ligands for ADGRG1 during OPC development.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phenotype in zebrafish mutants.

claim: ADGRG1 has been reported to undergo trans-trans homophilic interactions (i.e., interactions between ADGRG1 NTFs expressed on adjacent cells).
source: Additionally, ADGRG1 has been reported to undergo trans-trans homophilic interactions (i.e., interactions between ADGRG1 NTFs expressed on adjacent cells) (Paavola et al., 2011) and so it is also possible that ADGRG1N-hFc probe immunoprecipated ADGRG1 itself.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: TG2 can function as both GTPase intracellularly and crosslinking enzyme in the extracellular space.
source: TG2 can function as both GTPase intracellularly and crosslinking enzyme in the extracellular space (Lorand and Graham, 2003; Nakaoka et al., 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ADGRG1 activates RhoA to regulate OPC proliferation in a TG2-dependent manner.
source: This suggests that ADGRG1 activates RhoA to regulate OPC proliferation in a TG2-dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the RhoA activation data in Tgm2-/- mice.

claim: Microglial TG2 provides essential ligand activity for OPC-derived ADGRG1 during CNS myelination.
source: Here, we demonstrate that microglia-derived TG2 provides essential ligand activity for OPC-derived ADGRG1 during CNS myelination and that this signaling pathway is implicated in remyelination.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the combined experimental data.

claim: The ADGRG1-TG2 signaling pathway is implicated in remyelination.
source: Here, we demonstrate that microglia-derived TG2 provides essential ligand activity for OPC-derived ADGRG1 during CNS myelination and that this signaling pathway is implicated in remyelination.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the remyelination experimental data.

claim: A tripartite signaling complex comprised of microglial TG2, extracellular laminin, and OPC ADGRG1 regulates OL development and myelin repair.
source: Taken together, these findings show that the tripartite signaling complex comprised of microglial TG2, extracellular laminin, and OPC ADGRG1 regulates OL development and myelin repair.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the combined experimental data.

claim: TG2 interactions with ADGRG1 and laminin-111 may modulate ECM properties including stiffness, thus promoting OPC proliferation.
source: We speculate that TG2 interactions with ADGRG1 and laminin-111 modulate ECM properties including stiffness, thus promoting OPC proliferation (Jagielska et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic interpretation of the data.

claim: The same ADGRG1-TG2-laminin-111 signaling triad could also regulate OPC differentiation.
source: Although our study results support that ADGRG1-TG2-laminin-111 promotes OPC proliferation, it is possible that the same signaling triad could also regulates OPC differentiation. This model will be a subject of future investigation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential additional functions of the signaling pathway.

claim: TG2, contingent on its crosslinking activity and together with laminin-111, binds to the ADGRG1 NTF and initiates G-protein signaling.
source: We show that TG2, contingent on its crosslinking activity and together with laminin-111, binds to the ADGRG1 NTF and initiates G-protein signaling (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a mechanistic model supported by the combined experimental data and illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Activation of ADGRG1 in OPCs activates the small GTPase RhoA.
source: Activation of ADGRG1 in OPCs activates the small GTPase RhoA, a known downstream signaling protein, and additionally promotes the accumulation of the critical pro-mitotic cell cycle regulator CDK2.
evidence: This is supported by the RhoA activation and CDK2 protein level data.

claim: Activation of ADGRG1 in OPCs promotes the accumulation of the critical pro-mitotic cell cycle regulator CDK2.
source: Activation of ADGRG1 in OPCs activates the small GTPase RhoA, a known downstream signaling protein, and additionally promotes the accumulation of the critical pro-mitotic cell cycle regulator CDK2.
evidence: This is supported by the CDK2 protein level data.

claim: The finding that ADGRG1 activation promotes CDK2 accumulation is novel and offers new avenues of investigation into aGPCR-dependent regulation of cell cycle progression.
source: The latter finding is novel and offers new avenues of investigation into aGPCR-dependent regulation of cell cycle progression, a necessary step in generating OLs during myelination or remyelination.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the novelty and significance of the CDK2 finding.

claim: Modulating TG2 expression and/or secretion, or developing peptidomimetic drugs could represent viable therapeutic approaches in promoting remyelination.
source: Furthermore, modulating TG2 expression and/or secretion, or developing peptidomimetic drugs could represent as viable therapeutic approaches in promoting remyelination.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications.
